import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

t = np.linspace(0, 1, 500)  # uniform time points from 0 to 1 second
x = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2.0 * t)

clips.caption: First prepare the <c.aqua>time axis</c.aqua> and a 2 Hz reference <c.aqua>signal</c.aqua>.

actions.text:
A_ex = 0.8
f_ex = 1.5
phi_ex = np.pi / 4
x_ex = A_ex * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f_ex * t + phi_ex)  # plug the chosen A, f and phi into the sine formula

clips.caption: Put one working set of <c.aqua>amplitude</c.aqua>, <c.aqua>frequency</c.aqua> and <c.aqua>phase</c.aqua> into the same sine formula.

actions.text:
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
plt.plot(t, x, label="A=1, f=2 Hz, phase=0")
plt.plot(t, x_ex, label="A=0.8, f=1.5 Hz, phase=pi/4")
plt.title("One possible answer")
plt.xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.ylabel("Amplitude")
plt.legend()  # tell multiple curves apart
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

clips.caption: Draw the worked answer with the original <c.aqua>signal</c.aqua> and compare what the parameters changed.

Here is one working answer: A is 0.8, f is 1.5 Hz, phi is π/4. It is not the only answer; what matters is that you can explain the figure with <c.aqua>period</c.aqua>, <c.aqua>frequency</c.aqua> and <c.aqua>phase</c.aqua>.
